Soil degradation—the gradual decline in soil quality caused by improper land use, excessive
agrochemical application, and deforestation—poses a silent yet profound threat to global food
security. Healthy topsoil is not an inert mineral substrate; it is a living, biodiverse matrix teeming
with mycorrhizal fungi, nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and earthworms that cycle nutrients and retain
moisture. When intensive monoculture and deep mechanical tillage strip away organic matter, soil
structure collapses, accelerating wind and water erosion while diminishing water-infiltration
capacity. Reversing this trajectory necessitates regenerative agricultural practices such as cover
cropping, zero-tillage farming, crop rotation, and organic composting, which rebuild soil carbon
stocks and restore ecological resilience to farmlands.

Comprehension Passage – II (Questions 46 – 50): Read the following passage carefully and

The architectural evolution of Kalingan temple complexes between the seventh and thirteenth
centuries CE represents one of the highest pinnacles of Indian stone craftsmanship. Characterised
by the harmonious pairing of the curvilinear rekha deula (sanctum tower) and the pyramidal pidha
deula (assembly hall), Kalingan temples were constructed primarily using locally quarried sandstone
and laterite through dry-stone masonry, relying on precise interlocking ashlar blocks and iron
dowels rather than mortar. Beyond their structural ingenuity, the exterior facades of monuments
such as the Mukteswara, Lingaraja, and Konark Sun Temple served as encyclopaedic canvases of
sculptural narrative, depicting celestial musicians, flora, fauna, and scenes of everyday civic life.
Studying these monuments reveals not merely religious devotion, but a sophisticated synthesis of
structural engineering, geometry, and metallurgy.
